Write an element of a matrix in bold, with the matrix's own letter and its subscripts: $\matr{W}_{ij}$, not $W_{ij}$.
The bold letter then marks every symbol that stands for a matrix or a part of one,
so the reader never has to look up whether a letter names a matrix or a number.

This is the lab's convention.
Some textbooks write the elements of a bold matrix in plain italics,
for example $x_{ij}$ for an element of $\matr{X}$ [@james2021islr2, §1],
so a reader who knows those books will see a difference here.
Keep the bold form in every file you edit:
notes, assignments, solutions, slides and note sheets.

In a group that uses shared macros (see [Using shared macros](#using-shared-macros)),
write the element with the matrix macro: `\matr{W}_{ij}`.
Write a row or a column of a matrix, or a slice of it, the same way,
as in `\matr{U}_{1:L,\,:}`.

::: {#exm-matrix-elements}

## Writing a matrix element

> ❌ The hidden-layer weight $W_{ij}$ connects input $i$ to hidden unit $j$.
>
> ✅ The hidden-layer weight $\matr{W}_{ij}$ connects input $i$ to hidden unit $j$.

The ✅ version uses the same bold letter as the weight matrix $\matr{W}$,
so the element is visibly a part of that matrix.

:::
